h1: Opening a craft beer bar that buys from other breweries
title: Opening a Craft Beer Bar That Buys In | Craft Beer School
desc: How to open a craft beer bar that stocks other breweries: licence route, keg buying, cold room, draught lines, pricing per pour and menu rotation.
teaser: No brewhouse, no fermenters, but the same freshness problems. A bar that buys in lives or dies on its keg handling.
standfirst: A beer bar without a brewery is the cheapest way to start a craft beer business. It is also the one where you control the least. You choose the beers but you inherit every problem that happened before the keg arrived.
sections:
A bar that buys from other breweries sells selection and service. The brewery sells the beer. Your edge is a tap list people trust, kept in good condition, served by staff who can explain it. If that sounds modest, remember that most guests judge the bar by the pint in front of them, whoever brewed it.

The model has a real advantage over a brewpub. You skip the brewhouse spend and the brewing licence. Our guide on brewpub opening hours and staff shifts applies almost unchanged, because the bar side of the business is the same.

The disadvantage is margin and dependence. You pay a supplier's price and the supplier can run out, raise prices or open its own taproom nearby.
The licence and the supply route

In India alcohol is a state subject, so the licence you need to serve beer, the places you may buy from and the paperwork that follows every purchase differ between states. Some states let a bar buy directly from a licensed brewery. Others route purchases through a government depot or an authorised distributor. Rules change through notifications, so ask a licensing consultant for the current process before you sign a lease.

Do this first, because it decides whether the concept works. A bar that cannot legally buy the beers it wants has no menu. Our guide on buying craft beer kegs in Maharashtra shows what a buying route can look like in one state. Do not assume yours is the same.

Start with fewer taps than you think. Six to eight well chosen lines beat twelve that rotate slowly. Aim for range across the board: a pale lager, a wheat beer, a pale ale or IPA, something dark, something sour or fruity and one beer that suits people who say they do not like beer.

Buy from more than one brewery so a single outage does not empty a third of your taps. Ask each supplier about delivery days, minimum order, keg return terms and how fresh the beer will be on arrival. Unpasteurised draught beer is a perishable product. It needs cold storage from the brewery to your cellar.
The cold room is your brewhouse

Without a brewery, your cold room is where quality is won or lost. Kegs should sit at about 2 to 4 °C from the moment they arrive. A keg left on a loading bay for an afternoon in an Indian summer can warm well above 30 °C. Hoppy beers lose their aroma quickly in that state and others turn stale.

Plan the cold room for the volume you will hold on your busiest weekend, with room to rotate stock. Count the kegs you will keep on tap, in reserve and waiting to be returned. A cold room that is too small tempts staff to park kegs in the open.

Draught lines need cleaning, commonly at least every two weeks. A dirty line spoils good beer and the guest blames the brewery or the bar. Our guide to beer off flavours shows what a neglected line tastes like.
Price a pour, not a keg

Work out the cost of each glass, not the cost of the keg. Here is an illustration with round, made up figures. A 30 litre keg costs ₹12,000. Allow about 8% for foam, line loss and the last litre, which leaves roughly 27.6 litres. At 330 ml a pour that is about 84 glasses, so the beer costs about ₹143 a glass before rent, staff and every other cost.

Run the same sum for each beer on your own prices and your own glass sizes. Strong, expensive beers poured in small measures can make better margin than cheap beers poured in large ones. Never set a price by copying the bar next door.
Train the team to sell what you stock

The bar's advantage over a supermarket shelf is a person who can say what the beer tastes like. Staff should be able to describe every tap in a sentence, offer a taster measure where your rules allow and suggest something near a guest's usual choice. Our guide on training bar staff to sell craft beer sets out a plan.

Responsible service belongs in the same training: age checks, pacing, water on the table and no service to anyone who has had enough.

A beer bar has a simpler cost structure than a brewpub, but the maths of pour cost, stock holding and licence timing still decides survival. Brewery Business Management works through those numbers month by month, so you open with a plan that shows when the bar pays for itself.
faqs: Can a bar buy beer directly from a brewery in India?
It depends on the state. Some states allow it. Others route purchases through a government depot or an authorised distributor. Check the current notification or ask a licensing consultant.
How many taps should a new craft beer bar have?
Six to eight is a sensible start. A smaller tap list is easier to keep fresh and easier for staff to learn. Add taps once you know what sells.
How cold should kegs be kept?
About 2 to 4 °C from delivery to the glass. Warm storage ages beer quickly, especially hoppy styles.
How often should draught lines be cleaned?
Commonly at least every two weeks. Follow your equipment supplier's guidance and keep a written cleaning record.
